title: The secret in Bari harbor

facts.text: Bari, on Italy's Adriatic coast, was the main supply port for the British Eighth Army in December 1943 and home to the headquarters of the new U.S. Fifteenth Air Force. Few expected a German raid.

On the evening of 2 December 1943 about 105 Ju 88 bombers of the Luftwaffe's Luftflotte 2 came in from the east. The docks were brightly lit and the harbor was packed with ships. There was no time to get underway.
Between 17 and 28 Allied ships were sunk or destroyed, depending on the source. Five were American Liberty ships.
One was the SS John Harvey. In secret she carried 2,000 bombs, each filled with 60 to 70 pounds of sulfur mustard, a reserve to answer in kind if Germany used gas first. Hardly anyone ashore knew.
Burning debris set her alight and she blew up, killing everyone aboard. Mustard from the broken bombs mixed with the oil on the water and the billowing smoke.
Hospitals swamped with casualties left men in their oil soaked clothes. Hours later came burns, blisters and temporary blindness, and patients began to die in ways the doctors could not explain.

Lt. Col. Stewart F. Alexander, 29, a U.S. Army doctor trained in chemical warfare, was sent from Allied headquarters in Algiers. By mapping where each man had been and how he was burned, he traced the injuries to mustard.
When the diagnosis reached London, Winston Churchill replied that he did not believe there was mustard in Bari. The gas was kept secret, and deaths were recorded as burns due to enemy action.
More than 600 military and merchant marine men were treated for mustard exposure, and 83 of them died. Close to 1,000 civilians in the town were also killed in the raid.
Alexander's report recorded something new: in the gassed men, white blood cell counts collapsed, and lymphocytes were the first to disappear.

That finding fed the postwar push for cancer drugs. Cornelius Rhoads, former medical chief of the Chemical Warfare Service, saw it as a breakthrough. At Memorial Hospital in New York he pushed the search for mustard drugs that could kill cancer cells, and the Sloan Kettering Institute was announced in 1945.

Bari did not start chemotherapy alone. At Yale, a dying lymphoma patient had already received the first dose of nitrogen mustard on 27 August 1942, in wartime secrecy. Alexander's report added proof that the poison targeted the cells cancer doctors wanted to kill.

photoNote: Tier: green. Ships burning at the mole in Bari harbor after the raid of 2 December 1943, black smoke filling the frame. Narodowe Archiwum Cyfrowe (Polish National Digital Archives) sygn. 2-2442, photographer unknown, released by NAC under the Public Domain Mark; Commons marks it public domain. Saved 1920 x 900 from the Commons 1920 px thumbnail (original 3500 x 1690), cropped to remove the NAC reference strip at the bottom. Caution: the NAC print came through Wydawnictwo Prasowe Kraków Warszawa, the German run occupation press, so it is a wartime Axis press photo; it carries no agency mark and the archive released it as public domain, but Brian may prefer a U.S. photo. Chosen for drama: the only clear photo of the burning harbor that night or next morning. Runner up: NAC 2-2443, the companion frame (Commons). A U.S. Army photo of the burning ships (US Army Photo 155 6) is held by the National WWII Museum (ww2online.org/node/119034) but is not on Commons.

declassified.fact: Alexander already knew what nitrogen mustard did to blood. Working at Edgewood Arsenal in 1942, he had seen it drive the white cell counts of test rabbits to zero and dissolve their lymph nodes, and he proposed studying it as medicine. The idea was turned down.

film.shot_notes: Converted from NARA's WMV to H.264, 7 min 18 s, British narration, run silent. NOON: 01:14 to 01:44, German film: a Ju 88 formation in flight (01:14 to 01:30), a crewman in the glazed nose (01:18), Ju 88s passing low and diving over trees (01:34 to 01:44). Open on the formation at 01:14. 7 P.M. SECOND CUT: 00:54 to 01:12 German film of Ju 88s on their airfield, crews at work and a takeoff, then 01:46 to 02:08 clean low passes and a head on approach. Avoid the titles (00:00 to 00:20) and every stretch with white graphic outlines (02:10 to 02:34 and 02:40 onward).
film.date_note: Not film of Bari. German film of Ju 88s and British film of the type, used to show the bombers that made the raid. Caption: German film, from the British training film Recognizing the Ju 88 (1943).
